a0f61c6c0cf5cc52: From Khin Nadarajah and Sri Nadarajah
The 2027 budget brings fresh momentum to Malaysia’s preparations for longer lives.

Its wider investment commitments, including RM25 billion from government-linked investment companies, provide a timely setting to consider how capital, housing and care can work together for older Malaysians.

The opportunity is to translate that momentum into responsible investment in care, housing, healthcare, technology and services that families can depend on. The task is to turn that momentum into services that families can depend on.

The scale is clear. Asean’s population aged 60 and over stood at 74.4 million in 2020 and is projected to reach 127 million by 2035. The speed matters, too. France had 115 years to make the transition to an aged society. Malaysia will have about 27 years.

The statistics department's preliminary estimates for 2026 put the population aged 60 and above at 4.2 million, or 12.3% of the total. These figures make healthy ageing an immediate infrastructure and investment priority.

The recent call by the finance ministry to invest responsibly in the longevity economy remains an important starting point. As proposals take shape, it helps to keep their purpose in view: preserving independence, supporting changing needs and creating lasting value for both families and investors.
Care becomes investable when we can show that the service works for people as well as the numbers work for capital.
We should begin with the person rather than the building.

The National Health and Morbidity Survey 2025 found that 60% of older Malaysians were pre-frail, representing about 2.4 million people. Another 10.7% were already frail. This strengthens the case for earlier support, before greater dependency develops.

Most people hope to remain independent and connected to familiar surroundings for as long as they can. Their needs may then change gradually, or suddenly after an illness or a fall. A useful care system must offer choices between living at home with support and receiving more intensive help. Day services, rehabilitation, home nursing, assisted living and residential care each have a place.

The surroundings matter, too. A home that worked well at 45 may be harder to manage at 75. Stairs, maintenance, transport and access to healthcare can become obstacles. This does not necessarily mean someone needs residential care. It may mean the environment needs to adapt so that independence can continue.

The property sector, therefore, has a role beyond supplying more retirement units. Adaptable homes, accessible public spaces, walkable neighbourhoods and connections to health and community services can help people remain active and involved. Independence should be understood through the life a person can lead, as well as where they live.
This has consequences for development. A well-designed building matters, alongside its continuing usefulness as residents’ needs change.

Early collaboration with the care operator can help align design, skilled staffing and the support families may need over time. Clear information about services and costs helps families plan with greater confidence.
For families, the real test is simple: will this place still be right for someone they love when that person needs more help?

These considerations also strengthen the investment case. Local demand, sustainable pricing, staffing, governance and long-term maintenance deserve attention together. An adaptable, operationally viable development can better serve residents and sustain investor confidence.
The reduction in service tax on elderly care, together with the exemption announced in the 2027 budget, offers welcome relief for families.

They also provide a useful occasion to consider affordability across the full range of needs, from accommodation and daily living to more intensive care. Middle-income families and lower-income households should remain part of that planning. Affordability cannot be added as an afterthought.

Developers, care providers, insurers, employers and policymakers each have a role in exploring practical ways for people to pay for support across different stages of needs. Different households will need different arrangements. Community services, rental options and supported access can complement ownership models, where local evidence and sustainable funding support them.

The announced allocation of more than RM40 million to train 8,000 people in elderly care reinforces the importance of the workforce. Training, supervision and staff retention deserve the same early attention as land and buildings. Investing in people helps turn a well-designed setting into dependable and trustworthy care.
The proposed Senior Citizens Bill is a further reminder of the value of clear responsibility and accountability.
Safeguarding, transparent fees, accessible complaints procedures and standards that can be monitored help families, operators and investors build confidence together.

The same care should guide how progress is measured. Alongside beds built and units sold, attention should go to residents’ social connections, consistent care, timely support and staff development. These outcomes help show whether investment is adding value to everyday life.

One of us, Sri Nadarajah, was born in Malaysia and spent much of his working life developing businesses abroad. That experience taught him to respect both ambition and execution. A promising idea must survive contact with the practical details: land, finance, operations, people and accountability.
Malaysia does not need to choose between commercial discipline and doing good. The strongest care investments will require both.
The budget provides momentum; thoughtful partnerships can carry it forward. Institutional capital has a role alongside government, communities and responsible private operators.

With local evidence, adaptable design and clear delivery responsibilities, Malaysia can build homes and services that remain dependable as lives change. That is how longevity becomes part of the country’s working social infrastructure.

99bf30cc62cc4cf5: ‘We no longer see Nepali literature as something confined by geographical boundaries.’
Originally published on Global Voices
Rishi Ram Adhikari delivering a speech at the Kitab Jatra Festival held in London in August 2026. Photo by Kushal Shrestha. Used with permission.

The Kitab Jatra Festival has quickly become one of the most vibrant platforms for celebrating Nepali literature, books and culture. The Festival is organised and hosted by the Kitab Yatra Foundation, a Nepal-based organisation promoting literature, reading, art and cultural exchange. Since its launch in 2018, the festival has grown from a local gathering into a dynamic international event, connecting readers and writers not only across Nepal but also in India, the UK, and the USA, with plans to expand to Dubai, Australia, Portugal, Belgium and Germany. Working in collaboration with various organisations and institutions, it has created a global stage where Nepali voices are shared, celebrated and amplified.

At the heart of this movement is Rishi Ram Adhikari, Founder and Chairman of the Kitab Yatra Foundation and the Kitab Yatra book distribution company. In his early 30s, he emerged as a cultural entrepreneur dedicated to promoting Nepali literature and fostering a reading culture. His initiatives have not only expanded literary festivals abroad but also established over 20 libraries across Nepal and introduced scholarship programs for students.

Recognising these remarkable contributions, Kitab Yatra and Rishi Ram were honoured with the 5th edition of the Tally MSME Honours 2025 and the Public Choice ICT Award in 2019 for their pioneering efforts in enriching the Nepali literary world. This accolade further highlights his role as one of the leading advocates for Nepali literature today.
Sangita Swechcha from Global Voices interviewed Adhikari via email.
Sangita Swechcha (SS): What inspired you to start the Kitab Yatra book distribution company and the Kitab Jatra Festival at such a young age?

Rishi Ram Adhikari (RRA): My inspiration came from a simple but important realisation: books can transform individuals, and individuals can transform society. However, for that transformation to happen, books must be accessible, reading must become a habit and literature must be connected to people’s everyday lives.

Through Kitab Yatra, we began working to make books more accessible to readers across Nepal. But I gradually realised that distributing books alone was not enough. We also needed to create excitement around reading, bring writers and readers together, and make literature a part of public conversation. That realisation led to the Kitab Jatra Festival.

In my childhood, I listened to the chanting of my father reciting some slogans [from the epics] Mahabharat and Ramayan. While studying as a Chartered Accountant (CA) in New Delhi, India, despite my accounting career, I realised the value of words rather than numbers, so I dropped CA and came back to Nepal with four sacks of books and started an online bookstore in Kathmandu, Nepal. I believe young people should not wait for opportunities to create meaningful change; they should take the initiative to build them. Our journey has been driven by that belief, along with the dedication of our team, authors, partners and readers.
Book Exhibition at the 7th Edition of Kitab Jatra Festival in Nepal, December 2025. Photo by Kitab Jatra. Used with permission.
SS: How has the festival evolved since its beginnings in Nepal in 2018 to now being hosted in countries like the UK, USA, India, Portugal, Belgium, and Germany?

RRA: Since its beginning in 2018, Kitab Jatra has grown from a relatively small literary gathering into a broader platform for literature, culture and meaningful dialogue. What began with a limited number of voices and a single stage has developed into a festival bringing together writers, artists, thinkers, policymakers, entrepreneurs and readers from different generations.

The most important evolution has been in our ambition. We no longer see Nepali literature as something confined by geographical boundaries. Our international journey, including our work and outreach connected with the UK and other European countries, is an effort to connect Nepali writers with the diaspora and wider literary communities.

However, international expansion is not simply about taking a festival to another country. It is about building meaningful local partnerships, understanding the audience and creating a sustainable platform. Our goal is to make Kitab Jatra a bridge between Nepal and the world while ensuring that Nepali language, literature and cultural identity remain at its heart.
SS: What challenges do you face in promoting Nepali literature internationally, and how do you overcome them?

RRA: One of the biggest challenges is the limited international visibility of Nepali literature. We have talented writers, powerful stories, rich literary traditions and diverse cultural experiences, but many of these works remain inaccessible to international readers because of language barriers, limited translation opportunities, distribution challenges and insufficient global promotion.
Another challenge is sustainability. Organizing a meaningful literary festival requires financial resources, institutional partnerships, professional coordination and long-term commitment.

We are addressing these challenges by building partnerships with literary organizations, publishers, universities, diaspora institutions and cultural communities. We also want to encourage translation, book exchanges and conversations that introduce Nepali writing to audiences unfamiliar with our language and culture.

I believe we must move beyond simply asking the world to notice Nepali literature. We must create professional platforms, produce quality literary experiences and build lasting relationships that make such recognition possible. Our approach is to turn individual opportunities into long-term cultural connections.
Kitab Jatra Festival, 5th Edition Inaugural Session, New Delhi, India in February 2026. Photo Credit: Kitab Jatra. Used with permission.
SS: How do you see the role of the diaspora community in keeping Nepali literature and reading culture alive abroad?

RRA: The Nepali diaspora has a vital role in preserving and promoting our language, literature and cultural identity. For Nepalese living abroad, books can become a connection to their roots, history, memories, and sense of belonging. For younger generations growing up outside Nepal, literature can help them understand their heritage while encouraging them to explore their identity in a changing world.

I see the diaspora not merely as an audience but as an active partner in this literary journey. They can support Nepali authors, establish reading communities, organize literary discussions, introduce Nepali books to local libraries and connect our writers with international institutions.

Through Kitab Jatra’s international initiatives, we want to create spaces where these stories can travel across borders and where the diaspora can contribute to a living, evolving Nepali literary culture.
SS: Kitab Yatra Foundation has also been active inside Nepal, establishing libraries and supporting students — how do you balance its work at home and abroad?

RRA: For us, the work inside Nepal and our international initiatives are two sides of the same mission. We cannot talk about taking Nepali literature to the world while ignoring the need to make books accessible to people in our own communities.

Through our work in book distribution, library initiatives and student support, we aim to bring books closer to people — particularly those who have fewer opportunities to access them. Establishing libraries is not just about providing shelves and books; it is about creating spaces where curiosity can grow, young people can discover their potential, and communities can develop a lasting relationship with reading.

Internationally, we work to create visibility and opportunities for Nepali literature. At home, we work to strengthen the foundation from which that literature emerges. Balancing these responsibilities requires teamwork, partnerships and a clear sense of purpose.

Ultimately, success is not measured only by the size of a festival or the number of countries we reach. It is also measured by the child who discovers a love of reading, the student who receives an opportunity and the community that gains access to a library.
Written by Sangita Swechcha
8422634c9a069030: Today, a scientist who wants to simulate a physical process must pick the right tool for that one job, such as a solver built for flowing water or another designed to model the way a protein folds. Each one is hand-coded around the specific equations that dictate how that process behaves. Researchers at MIT, the University of British Columbia (UBC), and elsewhere have now replaced that patchwork with a single deep-learning system, called WorldParticle, that could help engineers model different physical phenomena, from sliding sand to folding proteins, with one unified artificial intelligence architecture. Scientists and engineers could use this system to model processes that typically require separate simulators, such as a fluid sloshing against a deformable solid. This could offer a faster, more accurate way to simulate how sloshing oil might impact an elastic valve in a storage tank, for instance. It could also help engineers study where and how granular materials, like sand or soil, could move when a soft robot touches them. The system represents every material it simulates, from a dune of sand to a protein molecule, as tiny particles and predicts where those particles will move one step at a time. Because it learns the underlying dynamics rather than being programmed with an equation, the model can adapt to materials, forces, and environments it never encountered during training.   In the long term, the researchers hope this work helps scientists discover new materials and explore physical processes they would be unable to effectively study with existing simulation methods. “We want to have a GPT moment for simulation,” says Peter Yichen Chen, a former MIT postdoc who is now an assistant professor at UBC, and is a co-corresponding author of an open-access paper on this technique. “Every time people want to build a simulator for a particular physical phenomenon, they need to code it up from scratch. Our vision is to have a foundation model that works out of the box for any scenario you want to simulate. This is a first step in that direction.” Chen is joined by co-corresponding and co-lead author Minghao Guo, an MIT postdoc; co-lead authors Caoliwen Wang and Siyuan Chen, UBC graduate students; Wojciech Matusik, an MIT professor of electrical engineering and computer science who leads the Computational Design and Fabrication Group within the Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL); and others at UBC, Georgia Tech, Inria, Meta, the University of Pennsylvania, the University of Utah, the University of California at Los Angeles, and the University of Hong Kong. The research will be presented at the ACM SIGGRAPH Conference and Exhibition on Computer Graphics and Interactive Techniques in Asia. Unified simulation For this work, the researchers drew inspiration from world models. These powerful AI systems learn the rules that govern the physical world so they can predict how objects or environments will change over time in response to certain actions or conditions. The researchers applied these concepts to develop a unified AI architecture that can simulate multiple types of physical phenomena.  “If you study deformable objects and fluids, you would need two simulators — one for each physical regime. But if you unify them into one model, maybe you could couple the physics of these two processes and gain insights into new problems?” Guo says. WorldParticle breaks an object into thousands or millions of tiny, three-dimensional dots, or particles, using what is known as a Lagrangian representation. It tracks the movement and velocity of the particles over space and time to simulate the material’s dynamics. Typically, when scientists model materials and physical processes using Lagrangian particles, they use a governing equation that defines the fundamental laws which control how that material behaves over time and space. They must convert that complex equation into a formula a numerical solver can handle, repeating these steps for each material and process they want to model. Instead, the researchers designed a neural network that learns to solve governing equations in general, eliminating the need to design a new model and solver to handle each one.  Once WorldParticle converts an object into particles, a neural network takes the 3D positions and physical properties of the particles as inputs. It outputs their positions and properties for the next frame of the simulation, predicting the material’s motion over time and space in one-second increments.  “It is a similar architecture to ChatGPT. But instead of predicting one word at a time to write a piece of text, we are predicting how these particles will move, one step at a time,” Chen says. Before each simulation step, WorldParticle separates the external forces that affect the physical system, like impulse forces that affect an ocean wave when it slams into a seawall.  After predicting the initial states of the particles, WorldParticle integrates the external forces back into the simulation, correcting its particle predictions based on how those forces affect the object’s behavior. In this way, the system can generalize to unseen materials, changing environmental conditions, and varied forces. A general, scalable framework But because a complex object could be broken into millions of particles, the problem quickly becomes too computationally intensive for the model to handle.  To streamline processing, the researchers employed a merging technique to combine and compress particles while still allowing WorldParticle to capture fine-grained details of their behavior. “We needed to do a lot of detailed engineering and employ many tweaks to the architecture for it to be truly generalizable and scalable,” Guo says. They demonstrated WorldParticle by modeling six different physical phenomena, including deformable objects, granular materials, and proteins, with higher accuracy than numerical simulation methods.  For instance, WorldParticle effectively captured how a granular object would collapse into a pile while some baseline methods left sand particles floating in the air. Their method also modeled how protein structures change over time about 100 times faster than numerical simulators, Guo adds.  The general-purpose framework could be applied to many materials and processes, including soft robot manipulation tasks, RNA evolution, and astrophysical phenomena like the merging of galaxies, the researchers say. Moving forward, they want to adapt WorldParticle to simulate these and other physical systems. They also want to build on this work toward the development of a full, general-purpose simulation pipeline for scientific discovery.   “We see the unification of computation and science giving us new insights and tools to discover physical phenomena or explain some unexplainable physical phenomena,” Guo says. “With a unified model, we could unlock many discoveries that we can’t even imagine.”
aac00f5f941f51b6: Humans are intuitive by nature. We can sense meaning beyond the literal words that we encounter. Now, a new artificial intelligence-assisted learning platform developed by MIT engineers is enabling robots to read larger meaning into a human’s natural language commands.  In a study to be presented at the annual Conference on Robot Learning this month, researchers from MIT and New York University introduce FLEX, a flexible feature-editing pipeline for robot motion-planning.  With FLEX, humans can interact with a robot by giving it instructions in natural, conversational language. The robot can not only follow the instructions literally but also read into the words to draw larger generalizations that help to improve its motion-planning task.  The team demonstrated FLEX in several simulated scenarios, including one in which a robot serves a cup of coffee. In these virtual scenarios, a person interacts with a robotic arm by typing commands in natural language. As the robot moves the coffee cup over a cluttered table, the person might type “Don’t spill on the laptop!” In response, the robot will reason about why it should avoid the laptop. For this, FLEX incorporates a large language model (LLM) — a type of AI system that is trained on enormous libraries of text, including social media posts, video transcriptions, and web content, which the LLM uses to identify larger trends, patterns, and generalizations.  “LLMs have seen so many texts from the internet,” says study author Nathan Dennler, a postdoc in MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL). “People might have written about, ‘Oh, my phone dropped in the water and now it doesn’t work,’ or ‘I spilled coffee on my computer and now it doesn’t work.’ So LLMs pick up on the idea that liquids plus devices leads to things not working.” Through the LLM, the robot reasons that it should also avoid bumping into all electronics. In its updated path, the robot adjusts to avoid both the laptop and a nearby phone, without the person having to explicitly spell this out. “The idea is that there is some higher-level intention behind the words that you say,” Dennler says. “People naturally get this. But you have to carefully explain that to a robot, which takes time and effort. FLEX gives you an interface of communication with a robot to say, ‘When people say this, they mean that.’” The study was led by Andreea Bobu, assistant professor of aeronautics and astronautics at MIT. Co-authors are Audrey Lee SM ’26 and Ilia Sucholutsky of New York University. Beyond what we say At MIT, Bobu heads up the Collaborative Learning and Autonomy Research (CLEAR) Lab, where her group develops autonomous agents that learn to work for, with, and around people. She is focused on developing assistive and household robots that can carry out physical tasks, and reason and adapt in real-time, in response to a person’s natural, conversational commands.  “Robots use math to do their trajectory planning. But we can’t expect a consumer to learn to do this math in order to tell a robot what to do,” says Dennler, who is a member of the CLEAR Lab. “Instead of having to get people to learn how to use a robot in a specific way, the goal is to interact with the robot through natural language.” There is a large effort in the robotics community to incorporate natural language into robotic learning pipelines. Various strategies include using language to clarify a task’s goal, redirect a robot’s trajectory, and update its understanding of what is a safe path to take. These existing methods use natural language to tell the robot how to physically perform a task. But a robot could potentially learn much more from what we tell it.  Bobu and her colleagues are expanding what robots can learn from natural language commands. In their new study, they focused on enabling a robot to interpret a person’s underlying, unspecified preference from limited natural language commands.   Absorbing common sense The team’s new robot learning platform, FLEX, is a three-step process that helps a robot read more into a natural language command, beyond what it is explicitly told to do.  The first step, “Add,” instructs a robot to add a feature to its list of things in its environment that matter for the task at hand, based on a user’s natural language command. For instance, as a robot is moving a bowling ball from one location to another, a person might interject with “Don’t drop it on my mug!” The robot would then add the mug to a list of things to avoid in its path. This first step is how previous methods have worked. Every time a person makes a correction, the robot adds to its features list, and updates its trajectory to avoid those features.  “The problem happens when your feature list becomes super long, and some features are no longer relevant because your environment may have changed,” says Dennler, who notes that this approach can grow tiresome if a person has to specify every specific feature to avoid.  The second step, “Generalize,” is the new solution that FLEX provides. This step incorporates an LLM — in this case, GPT-4o — that considers the mug, along with any other features that the person has so far specified to avoid. The LLM automatically searches through its vast cache of data for patterns and connections among these features, to ultimately make a generalization that it should avoid objects that are fragile, even when the person has not explicitly said so.  “LLMs have seen so many texts from the internet, from all sorts of people and places,” Dennler says. “Because they’ve trained so much on those things, some of that common sense gets absorbed into the LLM.” In the third step, “Mask,” the robot’s standard computer vision system assesses its environment to determine what objects are no longer present, and then deletes those objects from its features list. This entire three-step process takes about five seconds.  The team tested FLEX in simulations of a robot arm carrying out three different tasks: serving a cup of coffee, moving a candle, and carrying a bowling ball. In all three scenarios, volunteers interacted with the virtual robot by typing natural language commands, such as “Don’t spill on my laptop,” “Stay away from the stack of paper,” and “Don’t drop on the mug.” With FLEX, the robot followed all three commands literally and also reasoned at a higher level to not spill on electronics, stay away from flammable objects, and not drop its cargo on fragile things.  “Everyone’s homes are different, and everyone cares about different things, so no robot comes out of the box knowing what matters to you,” Bobu says. “What excites me about FLEX is that it can pick that up from a sentence or two instead of asking you to spell out every rule — and that’s the difference between a robot people put up with and one they actually want in their home.”  This work was partly supported by the MIT Generative AI Impact Consortium and the MIT Schwarzman College of Computing’s Social and Ethical Responsibilities of Computing program.

0a01fa9114296a5f: Tindakan membawa semula Najib Razak ke Penjara Kajang, yang terletak kurang 3km dari kediaman saya di Simpang Balak, mencetuskan kemarahan pelbagai pihak selepas Umno membayar denda RM50 juta dalam kes SRC International.
Sebahagian persepsi itu datang daripada Umno dan penyokongnya dalam Perikatan Nasional (PN) manakala sebahagian lagi daripada pejabat Yang di-Pertuan Agong.

Pada pandangan ramai, perintah pengampunan diraja itu cukup jelas. Sebaik sahaja Najib membayar denda RM50 juta, beliau sepatutnya dibawa pulang ke banglonya di Langgak Duta untuk menjalani tahanan rumah sehingga Ogos 2028, apabila hukuman penjaranya dalam kes SRC International berakhir.

Selepas itu, saya menjangkakan Najib kembali ke Penjara Kajang untuk menjalani hukuman penjara 15 tahun dalam kes 1MDB, selain membayar denda RM11 bilion. Saya juga mengandaikan Umno akan sekali lagi memohon pengampunan penuh atau pengurangan hukuman yang membolehkannya menjalani tahanan rumah sekali lagi.
Namun, adakah pelaksanaannya semudah disangka?

Ada beberapa perkara perlu difikirkan kerana isu tahanan rumah Najib ini mewujudkan satu duluan baharu dalam negara. Kita perlu memahami segala persoalan yang timbul dan mengambil pengajaran daripada keadaan yang masih tidak menentu ini.
Persoalan pertama saya ialah mengenai aspek keselamatan.
Dari sudut seni bina dan keselamatan bangunan, sejauh manakah sebuah kediaman atau banglo boleh diubah menjadi tempat tahanan yang benar-benar selamat?
Adakah rumah itu perlu diubah suai dengan memasang kunci keselamatan khas dan jeriji besi pada tingkap bagi menghalang tahanan melarikan diri dengan bantuan pihak luar?
Siapa tanggung kos?
Persoalan lebih penting ialah siapa yang akan menanggung kos pembaikan dan pengubahsuaian rumah itu?
Rumah itu milik Najib. Sebarang kerja pembaikan atau pengubahsuaian akhirnya akan memberi manfaat kepada pemiliknya.

Kerajaan pula hanya menggunakan kediaman itu sebagai tempat tahanan buat sementara sehingga Najib selesai menjalani hukumannya. Selepas itu, rumah berkenaan kembali sepenuhnya untuk kegunaan pemiliknya.

Namun, Najib tetap perlu kembali ke Penjara Kajang pada Ogos 2028, melainkan jawatan perdana menteri kembali ke tangan Umno dan parti itu berusaha mendapatkan pengampunan kali ketiga atau keempat untuknya.
Persoalan kedua saya membabitkan urusan lawatan, memandangkan rumah di Langgak Duta itu kini diwartakan sebagai penjara.
Setakat pemahaman saya terhadap arahan lembaga pengampunan, walaupun saya belum membaca minit mesyuaratnya, apa yang berubah hanyalah lokasi tahanan.
Justeru, persoalan yang semua pihak ingin tahu ialah apakah syarat dan peraturan akan dikenakan di penjara baharu ini?

Adakah Najib dibenarkan menerima kunjungan keluarga, ahli Umno atau PN dengan lebih bebas? Bolehkah pertemuan itu diadakan secara tertutup sehingga memberinya ruang merancang kemunculan semula dalam politik?

Adakah beliau juga dibenarkan menggunakan alat komunikasi elektronik untuk memuat naik swafoto ketika makan, membaca atau bersenam ringan, sekali gus kembali menjadi perhatian di YouTube menerusi fenomena Bossku 2.0?
Atau adakah Najib masih tertakluk kepada peraturan dan sekatan sama seperti ketika berada di Penjara Kajang?
Siapa penyumbang?
Persoalan ketiga saya berkaitan cara derma dikumpulkan bagi menjelaskan denda RM50 juta itu.

Jumlah kutipan yang begitu besar turut mewujudkan duluan tersendiri. Sukar bagi sesiapa yang berfikiran waras untuk mempercayai bahawa keseluruhan wang itu datang daripada ahli biasa atau mereka yang bersimpati dengan nasib Najib.

Ada pihak membayangkan individu tertentu bertanggungjawab menyediakan sumbangan yang tiba-tiba muncul dalam tempoh sehari, sedangkan sebelum itu tiada siapa menyangka jumlah berkenaan mampu dikumpulkan.
Apa yang kita dengar sebelum ini hanyalah pengumuman Setiausaha Agung Umno Asyraf Wajdi Dusuki bahawa RM10 juta berjaya dikumpulkan dalam tempoh dua minggu pertama.
Selepas itu, tiada perkembangan lanjut. Tiba-tiba, jumlah kutipan diumumkan sudah mencecah RM50 juta!
Turut timbul kebimbangan bahawa sumbangan itu mungkin sebenarnya berbentuk 'pelaburan' atau habuan daripada kroni Umno yang mengharapkan sesuatu sebagai balasan.
Keadaan ini menimbulkan persoalan mengenai aspek moral di sebalik kutipan derma tersebut.

Walaupun tiada undang-undang yang mewajibkan kempen kutipan derma diaudit, saya beranggapan perkara itu boleh dilakukan sekiranya seseorang membuat laporan polis atau kepada Suruhanjaya Pencegahan Rasuah Malaysia (SPRM).

Namun, jika tiada siapa tampil membuat laporan, kita memerlukan undang-undang yang dapat memastikan kempen kutipan derma bebas daripada sebarang penyelewengan supaya integriti dan kewajarannya dari sudut moral tidak dipersoalkan.
Keadaan seperti ini belum pernah berlaku sebelum ini, maka ia wajar diteliti dengan lebih mendalam.
Persoalan moral
Satu lagi perkara membimbangkan saya ialah implikasi agama apabila sumbangan diberikan kepada individu yang disabitkan kesalahan jenayah.
Melalui carian ringkas di internet, saya menemui satu fatwa yang menyatakan bahawa seseorang Muslim dibenarkan menghulurkan sumbangan bagi membantu individu yang disabitkan kesalahan.
Namun, ada syarat jelas yang perlu dipenuhi, iaitu individu berkenaan mesti mengakui kesalahannya dan menyatakan taubat secara terbuka.
Hanya selepas kedua-dua syarat itu dipenuhi, barulah bantuan kepada banduan tersebut dibenarkan.
Setakat pengetahuan saya, Najib masih belum memenuhi syarat taubat seperti yang dinyatakan itu. Jadi, apakah gambaran keadaan ini terhadap pegangan moral Islam di negara kita?
Persoalan terakhir saya ditujukan kepada sesiapa sahaja yang bakal menerajui negara ini.
Kita mengetahui bahawa ada sebuah parti politik yang mempunyai beberapa individu dalam kalangannya yang pernah didakwa atas kesalahan rasuah, termasuk pemimpin tertinggi dan presidennya sendiri.
Justeru, amat penting supaya segala peraturan berkaitan tahanan rumah diperjelaskan dengan sebaik-baiknya, tanpa meninggalkan sebarang ruang kekeliruan.
Malah, penjelasan itu mungkin menguntungkan bakal perdana menteri, menteri dan pegawai kerajaan pada masa depan.

Ini kerana pemimpin yang sedang memegang jawatan tinggi hari ini mungkin suatu hari nanti berdepan pendakwaan apabila kerajaan bertukar. Sekiranya itu berlaku, mereka juga boleh mengambil kesempatan daripada kemudahan tahanan rumah yang diwujudkan ini.

Atas sebab itu, saya memuji Jabatan Peguam Negara dan menteri dalam negeri kerana mengambil pendirian berhati-hati, walaupun langkah tersebut tidak popular, sebelum menetapkan duluan baharu di peringkat negara.
Selepas pilihan raya umum akan datang, malah apabila PRU17 tiba nanti, tidak mustahil negara akan mempunyai kerajaan baharu.
Ketika itu, tahanan rumah mungkin menjadi pilihan bagi lebih ramai pemimpin yang melanggar sumpah jawatan serta prinsip moral agama mereka.
Akhirnya, seperti kata pepatah, apa yang dilakukan seseorang mungkin suatu hari nanti berbalik kepada dirinya sendiri.
Artikel ini adalah pandangan penulis dan tidak semestinya mewakili FMT.
fcbff09be80281d7: A lot of anger has arisen since Najib Razak was returned to Kajang prison (barely 3km from my own residence in Simpang Balak), after Umno paid the RM50 million fine imposed as part of his sentence in the SRC International case.
Some of that anger came from Umno and its Perikatan Nasional supporters, and some from the office of the Yang di-Pertuan Agong.

To all and sundry, the royal pardon order was simple enough: once Najib has paid the RM50 million fine, take him back to his Langgak Duta mansion until August 2028, when his sentence in the SRC International case ends.

After that, I presume Najib would then be returned to Kajang prison to serve his 15-year sentence in the 1MDB case and pay his RM11 billion fine. I also assume Umno would then petition for a full pardon, or a partial one with yet another bout of house arrest.

But is this as straightforward as it sounds? There are several issues worth contemplating, as the issue of Najib’s house arrest has set a new precedent. We need to know, and grow from this uncertain prison situation.

My first question is about security. How secure is house arrest, in terms of converting a residence or mansion into a secure facility from an architectural perspective? Does the house need to be renovated with different locks and steel grilles on the windows, so that the prisoner is not able to escape with outside help?
Paying the bill

The more important aspect is: who pays the bill for house repairs and renovation? It is, after all, Najib’s house, and any repairs to it will benefit the owner. The government is only a temporary owner until Najib completes his prison sentence. After that, it is his house once again.
But, of course, he has to go back to Kajang prison in August 2028, unless Umno once again holds the prime minister’s post, as it will make sure of a third or fourth pardon session.

My second question is about visiting arrangements, since the house in Langgak Duta is now gazetted as a prison. As I understand the instructions of the pardons board, without having read the minutes, it calls for just a change of venue.
The question to which all of us are waiting to hear the answer is what the conditions will be at this prison.

Will Najib be able to entertain visits from family members, and Umno or PN members more loosely, and in private so that he can engineer his comeback? Can he access electronic communications to post selfies while eating, reading and exercising lightly, and become the latest YouTube sensation with Bossku 2.0?
Or is Najib subject to the same conditions as he was in Kajang prison?
Who made donations?

A third question about the way donations were made to pay the RM50 million fine. As the amount collected is so large, it sets a precedent of its own: no sane person would believe it came from ordinary members or those sympathising with Najib's situation.

It has been suggested that certain people were responsible for the "donation” that suddenly materialised in a single day, when no one had even guessed that it could happen. We only heard Asyraf Wajdi Dusuki announce that RM10 million was collected within the first two weeks, and then silence. After that, boom, RM50 million was collected!
There have also been concerns that the donations could be some kind of “investment”, or even kickbacks from Umno cronies. This brings into question the morality of the donation..

Although no law requires a donation drive to be audited, I assume it could be done if someone were to make a police or MACC report. But if none comes forth to lodge any reports, then we need a law that says there can be no hanky-panky in donation drives, in order to have some sense of palatable morality regarding the case.
This situation is a first and thus needs some scrutiny.
A matter of morality

An additional concern is regarding the religious implication of making donations to a convicted felon. From a simple search online, I found that a religious fatwa was made stating that a Muslim can donate to help a clearly convicted felon - with the clear condition that he or she admits to the crime and pronounces repentance in public. Then, and only then, is it permissible to help the prisoner.
Since Najib has not fulfilled the religious condition of repentance, as far as I know, where does that leave this country’s Islamic moral compass?
My final question is for whoever is going to lead this country.
One political party is known for having among its ranks people who have been indicted for corruption - not only several members, but also its highest-ranking member and president himself.

It would be to the advantage of future prime ministers, ministers and officials that the house arrest issue be clarified in a crystal clear manner, because the same leaders holding high office could then use this “facility” should their possible indictment occur under a future government.

I therefore applaud the Attorney-General's Chambers and the home minister for taking the unpopular stance of caution before setting this new national precedent. After the coming general election, and when GE17 then comes around, there may be a new government in place, and this issue of house arrest may once again be the fate of many more leaders who transgress their oath of office and religious morality.
Alas, as the saying goes, what goes around eventually comes around.

7f152ca6be50c785: From Moaz Nair

For generations, higher education functioned as a cornerstone of the Malaysian social contract. A tertiary degree, achieved through rigorous academic adherence, effectively guaranteed upward socioeconomic mobility and entry into the professional middle class.
Today, however, structural shifts induced by advanced automation and artificial intelligence have fundamentally fractured this predictable linear trajectory.

While aggregate macroeconomic indicators present a resilient domestic economy, micro-level data from the labour market reveals a systemic disruption. The proliferation of generative AI tools has effectively dismantled the entry-level tier of corporate employment, placing the return on investment of a traditional university degree under severe scrutiny.
Are educators in our higher educational institutions prepared to embrace this technology?

Data from the statistics department illustrates the depth of this structural paradox. While the national unemployment rate stands at a remarkably healthy 2.9%, youth unemployment (ages 15 to 24) remains stubbornly elevated at 10.1%, representing approximately 291,300 young citizens experiencing market-entry barriers.
Of more concern is the pervasive rise of skills-related underemployment.

According to the latest graduate statistics, 32.2% of the employed graduate workforce, or 1.6 million people occupy roles categorised as semi-skilled or low-skilled. The visual narrative of tertiary-educated youth operating within the gig economy or basic service sectors rather than corporate offices is no longer an anomaly; it is an empirical trend.
Young people who would normally have gone into routine professional jobs are now serving customers in tea shops. This is not what our youth aspire to.

Historically, entry-level positions served a dual purpose: they fulfilled corporate administrative needs while acting as a vital practical apprenticeship for fresh graduates. Tasks such as data compilation, minute-taking, draft formulation, and presentation synthesis allowed new entrants to internalise corporate culture, systemic hierarchies, and operational soft skills.

With AI software now executing these routine, algorithmic tasks at a fraction of the temporal and financial cost, private firms are actively reducing their junior headcounts and altering hiring thresholds.

Emerging market analysis suggests that up to 40% of standard roles historically allocated to fresh graduates have undergone severe contractions due to routine automation. Consequently, universities face an immediate existential mandate.
Institutions can no longer function as passive, credential-issuing entities, or they risk producing graduates equipped only with obsolete paper qualifications.

To prevent a structural underemployment crisis from solidifying into permanent socioeconomic inequality, a comprehensive paradigm shift must occur across institutional curricula. The traditional instructional methodology predicated on stagnant, rote-learning lectures and memory-based assessments is fundamentally incompatible with an economy wherein raw information retrieval is instant and costless.

Higher education institutions must intentionally pivot towards developing capabilities that lie beyond the current frontier of machine learning. This requires an academic focus on high-order cognitive processes, including multi-system thinking, advanced cross-disciplinary innovation, ethical governance, and sophisticated emotional intelligence.

Recognising the urgency of this transition, the higher education ministry has proactively initiated key systemic changes, recently undertaking a comprehensive review of 455 public university study programmes.

The ministry has set an aggressive target to integrate foundational AI components into 80% of all public undergraduate courses, alongside the ongoing expansion of specialised entities like the Faculty of Artificial Intelligence at Universiti Teknologi Malaysia.
The broader national blueprint aims to generate 30,000 highly skilled AI graduates by 2030 to mitigate the effects of rapid workspace automation.

However, transforming formal degree structures is merely one component of a holistic strategy. A real-world equilibrium requires immediate, coordinated fiscal and policy interventions executed in tandem with industry demands. To successfully navigate this transition, public and private stakeholders must scale up initiatives across three essential pillars.

First, academic faculties must build institutionalised, dynamic bridges with corporate partners. This collaboration ensures that university modules adjust symmetrically alongside rapidly evolving technological frontiers, shifting student assessment metrics toward practical problem-solving.

Second, leveraging national frameworks like the New Industrial Master Plan 2030 and substantial public sector technology allocations, universities must aggressively channel funds into high-performance computing infrastructure, advanced hardware acquisition, and research commercialisation funds.

Finally, stakeholders must expand lifelong reskilling ecosystems. This means scaling up structural upskilling pipelines such as micro-credentials and technical courses certified by agencies like TalentCorp or funded through HRD Corp to swiftly transition underemployed or displaced workers into high-growth, non-routine fields like semiconductor IC design, cybersecurity, and digital health.

The proliferation of artificial intelligence software does not inherently dictate the obsolescence of the university system; rather, it demands its radical re-engineering. If higher education institutions fail to adapt, the domestic economy risks widening its structural inequalities, trapping a large segment of the domestic talent pool in low-value service roles while a thin, technologically elite class captures the premium of digital growth.

Higher education must act with proactive foresight and structural courage. By transforming the curriculum from a static knowledge repository into a dynamic incubator for uniquely human innovation, Malaysian universities can ensure that their graduates remain the primary architects of the national digital economy.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.

a389df548db6df1c: This has been an era of shocks. In the space of two decades, the world has witnessed globally disruptive wars—from Iraq in the 2000s to Ukraine and Iran today—a global financial crisis, a global pandemic, and a rogue American president upending the global order.
Now, yet another potential shock must be addressed: Though few dare to speculate about it publicly, an economic and political perfect storm is bearing down on China.
On the political front, Chinese president Xi Jinping has ruthlessly eliminated all potential opposition and centralised power in his own hands.

His decimation of the state, party, provincial, and military leadership has left a trail of bodies and resentment, even if the impenetrability of the Communist Party of China (CPC) makes this difficult to establish definitively.
With blood and revenge hammering in their heads (to paraphrase Shakespeare), numerous humiliated and disgruntled former officials could make Xi’s succession, whenever it comes, disorderly.

Cycles of apparent calm leading to chaos are not uncommon in Chinese history. They are intrinsic to what Francis Fukuyama has called the country’s “Bad Emperor” problem, with Mao Zedong and Xi representing the bad emperors of the Communist era.

On the economic front, the outlook is mixed, but downside risks are growing. Where some see an all-conquering powerhouse marrying technology to mass manufacturing, others see an economy dragged into a structural slowdown by population ageing, a prolonged property market slump, rising youth unemployment, and growing hostility to private enterprise.

Making matters worse, the long-standing source of Chinese dynamism—exports—is vulnerable to policy responses from the US and Europe, which are under immense pressure to address the latest China shock.

But perhaps even more worrying is China’s fraying fiscal capacity. Warnings about unsustainable public debt are growing louder everywhere, but the situation in China is distinctive, owing to how it manages—or, rather, fails to manage—taxation.

Few states are as successful as China when it comes to surveilling and controlling the population. But taxes represent a reciprocal bargain with citizens, who accept expropriation as legitimate on the understanding that they will get something in return: stability, public goods, improved standards of living, redistribution, and so forth. That is why wars and even empires can be lost when a state loses its capacity to tax its citizens.
The fate of the Ming and Qing dynasties is telling in this respect. Even discounting for the obvious historical differences, these episodes have faint echoes in developments today.

We recently mapped China’s taxes and revenues since 1952. Two features stand out. First, and somewhat surprisingly, the CPC has not presided over a particularly strong fiscal state. Instead, it has raised a substantial share of resources without explicitly taxing its people.

Until the late 1970s, about half the resources raised came from profits of state-owned enterprises; and in the last two decades, about one-sixth (and as much as one-quarter at its peak in 2020) has come from land sales.
In other words, China has never managed to raise sufficient sums of money via personal income taxation, even during a period of extraordinary economic vibrancy.

Over the last decade, its tax revenues from the personal income tax averaged just 1.2% of GDP. Ironically, a communist state ideologically committed to collective ownership of the means of production has had to raise revenue by divesting itself of that most sacred input, land. Evidently, the CPC can make the Chinese cower in silence, but finds it difficult to reach into their pocketbooks.
The second and even more relevant finding is that, regardless of how they are measured, revenues and taxes have been declining for about a decade.

For example, taxes (excluding social-insurance contributions) collapsed by nearly six percentage points between 2012 and 2025, from 18.4% of GDP to 12.6%. These are levels associated with a struggling, lower-middle-income country, not an aspiring superpower.
It is difficult to say how much of this decline is attributable to growth falling below what headline figures indicate, and how much to weakening enforcement capacity.

Either way, it seems that the government grew so reliant on nontax revenues that it found itself with no options when they dried up. Whether it can change course and impose taxes on the population very much remains to be seen.
The Chinese state could find itself triply exposed—to a succession crisis, a weakening economy, and a lack of resources to exercise power domestically and project it externally.

In short, China’s entire growth and fiscal model, along with the social contract between the state and its citizens—coveted stability and material prosperity for restricted freedom and muzzled voice—may be in trouble.
Of course, any warning about China’s potential descent into disorder must contend with the CPC’s remarkable record of coercive control.

A slow bleed of anemic growth, rising restiveness, and deteriorating services is perhaps likelier. But even if the Chinese miracle ends with a whimper rather than a bang, the consequences may well be yet another global shock.
Navneeraj Sharma is an energy economist. Arvind Subramanian is a senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics.

bb81a080181292fa: Di Malaysia hari ini ada suatu dilema yang mempunyai implikasi besar terhadap bagaimana Islam perlu dipelajari dan didakwahkan. Ia merangkumi isu derma untuk membayar saman fitnah seorang ahli politik dari parti yang dilaungkan sebagai pejuang Islam, dan derma untuk melunaskan denda hukuman rasuah seorang pemimpin parti politik yang melaungkan kaum Melayu sebagai perjuangan utama.

Dari pemerhatian saya, kalau kes fitnah dan rasuah itu bersifat circumstantial atau agak pudar dan banyak lubang pembuktian, saya tidak akan menulis artikel ini kerana derma bagi kedua-duanya boleh saja dihalalkan dari kaca mata perjuangan Islam atau nasional, tetapi dari apa yang saya faham tentang bukti dan pembicaraan kes-kes, semuanya sahih dan terbaik maka tidak ada keraguan dalam proses pengadilan. Namun demikian, derma untuk membayar saman fitnah dan derma untuk bantu bayar denda hukuman rasuah telah dilancarkan. Yang peliknya penjawat rasmi agama, pendakwah terkenal agama dan profesor agama sepi terhadap sama ada praktis sedemikian layak dikaitkan dengan nilai Islam. Maka itu, terpaksalah saya menulis sesuatu sebagai semacam peringatan.

Sebagai seorang yang telah membina kesedaran Islam di Amerika Syarikat sewaktu belajar jurusan seni bina di bawah tajaan JPA, saya telah menambah banyak ilmu tentang Islam melalui pembacaan koleksi hadis seperti daripada Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, Muwatta, Tirmidhi, An-Nasai dan Ibn Madjah, serta menelaah tafsiran al-Quran oleh Muhammad Assad, Abdullah Yusof Ali, Hamka dan Abul A'la Maududi. Penelitian peribadi ini membawa saya kepada banyak buku tentang kerohanian, politik dan aspek sosial Islam. Dalam banyak bacaan saya, ayat dari surah al-Baqarah ini menjadi pedoman kepada saya tentang 'politik Islam';

"Bukanlah perkara kebajikan itu hanya kamu menghadapkan muka ke pihak timur dan barat, tetapi kebajikan itu ialah berimannya seseorang kepada Allah, dan hari akhirat, dan segala malaikat, dan segala kitab, dan sekalian nabi; dan mendermanya seseorang akan hartanya sedang ia menyayanginya, -- kepada kaum kerabat, dan anak-anak yatim dan orang-orang miskin dan orang yang terlantar dalam perjalanan, dan kepada orang-orang yang meminta, dan untuk memerdekakan hamba-hamba abdi; dan mengerjanya seseorang akan sembahyang serta mengeluarkan zakat; dan perbuatan orang-orang yang menyempurnakan janjinya apabila mereka membuat perjanjian; dan ketabahan orang-orang yang sabar dalam masa kesempitan, dan dalam masa kesakitan, dan juga dalam masa bertempur dalam perjuangan perang Sabil. (Orang yang demikian sifatnya), mereka itulah orang yang benar (beriman dan mengerjakan kebajikan); dan mereka itulah juga orang yang bertaqwa. (al-Baqarah ayat 177)

Dari ayat ini saya boleh membina masyarakat yang baik, saya boleh membina hubungan kerohanian dengan tuhan dan saya juga boleh merancang sebuah perbandaran serta seni binanya untuk manusia. Ayat ini cukup meyakinkan saya kepada apa sebenarnya politik Islam iaitu memimpin manusia ke arah kemanusiaan sejati.

"Bukanlah perkara kebajikan itu hanya kamu menghadapkan muka ke pihak timur dan barat, tetapi kebajikan itu ialah berimannya seseorang kepada Allah, dan hari akhirat, dan segala malaikat, dan segala kitab, dan sekalian nabi; dan mendermanya seseorang akan hartanya sedang ia menyayanginya" memberi definisi 'kebaikan' atau righteousness iaitu bukan sekadar ibadah ritual tetapi merangkumi suatu kesejagatan kemanusiaan di mana orang Islam perlu berkawan dengan semua manusia yang mempercayai konsep ketuhanan, penghakiman akhir, kewujudan malaikat dan pendidikan melalui kitab-kitab lama berkait dengan rasul-rasul yang kita semua umat Islam kena hafal nama dan kewujudan mereka. Kita pun tahu bahawa sejarah rasul-rasul berkait rapat dengan sejarah dan kepercayaan agama Yahudi dan Kristian. Saya memahami bahagian pertama ini sebagai suatu ajakan untuk umat Islam bersaudara dengan penganut dua agama tersebut. Namun demikian kita kini berseteru dengan kedua-duanya dari sudut politik kenegaraan.

"...dan mendermanya seseorang akan hartanya sedang ia menyayanginya, -- kepada kaum kerabat, dan anak-anak yatim dan orang miskin dan orang yang terlantar dalam perjalanan, dan kepada orang yang meminta, dan untuk memerdekakan hamba-hamba abdi" bagi saya adalah tentang suatu sistem sosial yang bukan sahaja untuk sesebuah negara yang mengamalkan hukum dan nilai Islam tetapi juga tanggungjawab setiap muslim untuk membantu golongan yang berkeperluan seperti anak yatim piatu, musafir, yang meminta dan yang memerlukan bantuan kerana keperitan hidup. Kadang-kadang saya hairan apabila dalam sesebuah bandar yang dipimpin orang Islam ada ribu rakyat homeless berbagai kaum tetapi kita punyai rumah ibadat seperti masjid, gereja, kuil dan sebagainya dalam jumlah beratus buah. Sebagai umat kita lebih suka melihat bangunan ibadat beratus juta kecantikannya tetapi membiarkan yang berkeperluan merana sendiri. Siapa agaknya kena jawab di akhirat nanti.

"...dan mengerjanya seseorang akan sembahyang serta mengeluarkan zakat; dan perbuatan orang yang menyempurnakan janjinya apabila mereka membuat perjanjian; dan ketabahan orang yang sabar dalam masa kesempitan, dan dalam masa kesakitan, dan juga dalam masa bertempur dalam perjuangan perang Sabil. (Orang yang demikian sifatnya), mereka itulah orang yang benar (beriman dan mengerjakan kebajikan); dan mereka itulah juga orang yang bertakwa" saya fahami sebagai hubungan peribadi kita dengan Tuhan dalam ibadat khusus seperti bersembahyang, dan merenggangkan kita dengan harta benda sebelum kita menemui-Nya. Umat Islam juga diseru untuk menjadi profesional dalam muamalah perjanjian dan tanggungjawab antara manusia tidak kira dari kaum mana atau agama apa, saya kira.

Dalam surah al-Baqarah ayat 177 jelas tiada berkeperluan kita umat Islam untuk merenggangkan kita dengan harta dan wang demi membantu derma bagi membayar saman fitnah yang jelas terbukti tanpa was-was serta juga menderma kepada pembayaran denda hukuman rasuah yang juga terjelas tanpa was-was proses keadilannya.
Jadi, untuk kita orang Melayu dan Islam kat mana atau 'tang' mana kita nak selit amalan kita untuk menjayakan hidup sebagai Muslim yang sejati dan ikhlas membuat kebaikan?

Kalau parti-parti yang menghadapi musibah lalu ahli dan pemimpinnya menggunakan wang tabung parti sendiri tanpa derma maka boleh juga diterima alasan 'strategi politik' agar tidak hilang kerusi dan tidak merendahkan maruah ahli serta parti, walaupun konsep nilai Islam masih lagi boleh dipersoalkan. Tetapi melancarkan derma dan mengajak 'kebajikan' daripada umat Islam untuk 'membantu' musibah yang al-Quran tidak pernah sebut, itu suatu perkara yang cukup problematic dalam usaha menguar-uarkan Islam sebagai agama kemanusiaan terbaik. Walaupun Jabatan Mufti Wilayah Persekutuan ada buat fatwa bahawa membantu orang yang didapati bersalah oleh mahkamah hukumnya harus, tetapi ia bersyarat iaitu si pesalah perlu mengaku kesalahan dan bertaubat tidak akan membuatnya lagi. Saya tak dengar pun Dr Siti Mastura Muhammad atau Najib Razak berbuat demikian.
Kalau dulu ada buku 'Dilema Melayu', saya kira tiba masanya ada buku 'Dilema Muslim' untuk sama-sama kita renungkan pengakhiran kita dan negara.
Artikel ini adalah pandangan penulis dan tidak semestinya mewakili FMT.
b5623db3fc4b9902: From Zander Lim

Recent criminal breach of trust (CBT) prosecutions involving corporate directors, senior executives and individuals entrusted with institutional funds have renewed attention to the distinction between corporate mismanagement and criminal liability.
Among these are recent prosecutions involving former executives of UiTM Holdings Sdn Bhd and companies associated with Lembaga Tabung Haji.
These cases raise an important legal question: Does an unauthorised financial transaction, breach of corporate procedures or failure of governance necessarily constitute CBT?

In 2026, several CBT prosecutions were reported, including those involving a former senior military officer in relation to RM3 million belonging to the Armed Forces welfare fund; two company directors involving RM10.55 million connected with a glove manufacturing venture; former executives of three companies concerning contractor penalty payments; and the former CEO of UiTM Holdings Sdn Bhd involving approximately RM37.37 million allocated for a solar photovoltaic project.
The accused persons have pleaded not guilty, and the allegations remain subject to judicial determination.

Although these prosecutions involve different transactions and circumstances, they raise important legal questions concerning entrustment, corporate authority and the element of dishonesty required to establish criminal breach of trust.
What is criminal breach of trust?
In simple terms, CBT occurs when a person entrusted with someone else's money or property dishonestly misuses it.
Under Section 405 of the Penal Code, the prosecution must generally prove three matters:
(a) Entrustment: the accused was given responsibility for, or control over, the money or property.
(b) Misuse: the accused used or dealt with it in a manner prohibited by law.
(c) Dishonesty: the accused acted dishonestly, rather than merely making a mistake or exercising poor judgment.
Section 409 provides heavier punishment where CBT is committed by certain persons, including public servants and agents.
Importantly, not every unauthorised payment or breach of company procedures amounts to CBT. Dishonesty must still be established.
When does mismanagement become a criminal offence?
Companies may suffer financial losses arising from poor investment decisions, inadequate due diligence, improper approvals or failures in corporate governance.
However, a bad business decision is not necessarily a criminal offence.

For example, Illustration (d) to Section 405 recognises that a person who acts contrary to instructions but genuinely believes the decision would benefit the owner of the property may not have committed CBT, although civil liability may arise.
Conversely, Section 409A makes clear that recording a transaction in the company's accounts does not automatically protect a person from criminal liability.
In other words, a transaction is not necessarily criminal merely because company procedures were breached, nor is it necessarily lawful simply because it was properly recorded or approved.
What matters is whether the money or property was dishonestly misused in circumstances falling within Section 405.
Corporate seniority
In corporate organisations, financial decisions often involve several levels of management, including directors, finance departments and authorised signatories.

Holding a senior position does not necessarily mean that an individual controlled every company transaction. Similarly, approving a payment does not automatically establish dishonest misappropriation.

In determining whether CBT has been committed, consideration must be given to the accused's control over the funds, the purpose of the transaction, the scope of authority and whether the evidence establishes dishonest intention.

In cases involving abetment under Sections 107 and 109 of the Penal Code, criminal liability cannot be established merely because an individual occupied a supervisory position or participated in an approval process.
The prosecution must establish the relevant acts and legal requirements constituting abetment.
Criminal liability must be based on the individual's actual conduct, not merely the position he or she held.
The recent CBT prosecutions highlight the importance of proper financial controls, clear approval procedures and accountability in corporate management.
Nevertheless, financial irregularities, breaches of internal policies and unsuccessful business decisions do not automatically amount to criminal wrongdoing.
Ultimately, the distinction between corporate mismanagement and CBT is not determined by the amount of money involved, the seniority of the accused or whether company procedures were breached.
It depends on whether the accused dishonestly misused money or property entrusted to him or her in a manner prohibited by law.
This distinction is essential to ensuring that genuine criminal misconduct is addressed without treating every failure of corporate governance as a criminal offence.
Zander Lim is an advocate solicitor and managing partner of Law Chambers of Zander Lim.

c6db132144c32013: Diego Radames/GettyThis week, around 80 world leaders – including Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese – will descend on the coastal Turkish city of Antalya for the annual United Nations climate summit, COP31. For the first time, the summit duties will be shared; Turkey will play host, while Australia leads negotiations. At home, these national leaders have no shortage of issues to contend with: the challenges of AI, major wars and declining trust in democracy. Yet looming over all of them is the existential threat posed by a heating planet. Climate change is a truly global challenge. Greenhouse gases have no respect for national boundaries, and the devastating impacts are being felt everywhere. We don’t have a world government, but we do have processes of international diplomacy to hammer out shared commitments. This is how the world is trying to deal with the climate crisis. It can be easy to be pessimistic, but COP31 can still deliver real progress. In Antalya, countries will consider a global electrification target to hasten the shift from coal, oil and gas toward clean electricity. If agreement can be found, this will be a major step forward. Remind me, what is a COP? When scientific consensus emerged on global warming in the 1980s, countries negotiated and signed a new framework on climate change in Rio De Janeiro in 1992. Since then, diplomats and negotiators have met annually for the UN’s Conference of Parties (COP) to discuss how to address dangerous human-made climate change. These talks have become huge, attended by tens of thousands of delegates every year. This year, the 31st COP is being held in Antalya, Turkey. After three decades of climate talks, countries are turning the tide on emissions. Many are transitioning away from fossil fuels, if not at the speed required. Overall, global emissions held roughly flat in 2025, though lower wildfire and land-use emissions masked continued growth from fossil fuels. Yes, the annual UN climate talks are beset by challenges. The United States has withdrawn completely. Countries are not on track to limit warming to agreed levels. Governments can’t even agree when to release the next report on global warming to guide negotiations. In some ways it’s a miracle these talks achieve anything. Agreements must be reached by consensus and endorsed by 190-plus countries, from petro-states in the Middle East to vulnerable island nations in the Pacific. Consensus is both strength and weakness. When agreements are reached, they have great legitimacy. The 2015 Paris Agreement came after two decades of hard-fought negotiations. The agreement was a monumental achievement. But consensus also means COP decisions tend to be “lowest-common-denominator” outcomes, representing incremental progress. Again and again, politics and diplomacy fall short of what the science says is required. Still, if we take a long view, we can see the UN climate talks have helped avoid the most catastrophic global warming and are transforming economies. A demonstrator holds a banner showing the 1.5°C mark, as demonstrators march past the Reichstag building in Berlin, Germany, in April to protest for renewable energies. The UN has confirmed the world will overshoot 1.5°C in the next few years. Photo by Omer Messinger/Getty Images How the Paris Agreement is working At the heart of the Paris Agreement is the goal of limiting warming to 1.5°C above the long-term average. This requires the global economy to get to net-zero emissions by the middle of this century. To get there, countries agreed to set emissions targets and increase these every five years. While these targets are slowly cutting emissions and limiting warming they are still clearly insufficient. Before the Paris Agreement, the world was on track for a cataclysmic 4°C degrees of warming this century. The first wave of emissions targets brought this below 3°C. The 2025 round of targets suggests countries may limit warming to 2.6°C. Every fraction of a degree matters. With more ambitious policies, we could theoretically still peak warming at 1.8C and return below 1.5°C later this century through investment in carbon dioxide removal. However, this would take a radical step-change in ambition. Since Paris, more than 130 countries have set long-term targets to achieve net-zero emissions. Countries have begun to signal the end of the fossil fuel era. At COP26 in Glasgow in 2021, countries agreed to “phase down coal”. At COP28 in Dubai in 2023 they agreed to “transition away from fossil fuels”. The task now is to make good on these promises. Taken together, COP commitments act as a market signal. This year, global investment in clean energy hit A$3.2 trillion – twice as much as investment in coal, oil and gas. Renewables also overtook coal as the world’s biggest source of electricity. A new age of electricity For COP31, there is a push for an electrification target of “35 by 35”. Both Turkey and Australia are pressing for a global commitment to increase the share of the energy delivered to consumers by electricity, from just over 20% today to 35% by 2035. It sounds wonkish, but could usher in a new age of electricity. A shift to electric vehicles, electric heating and cooling, and modernised heavy industry will cut emissions while slashing global fossil fuel import bills by $720 billion each year. An electrification target may also be easier to land than agreement to phase out fossil fuels. Ironically, given his support for the oil industry, US president Donald Trump has made perhaps the clearest case for electrification. The US war on Iran has triggered the largest disruption of oil supply in history. Demand for clean energy technologies is surging as countries seek alternatives to volatile fossil fuel imports. The exact form of an electrification target at COP31 will be subject to intense negotiations. Australian climate minister Chris Bowen will have his task cut out for him as chief negotiator. In itself, COP31 can’t deliver a silver bullet for climate action. But if it reinforces international cooperation and moves the dial forward on global electrification, hope remains. Wesley Morgan is a fellow at the Climate Council of Australia

(Imperial War Museums)Who do we forget on Remembrance Day? For a long time, histories of the First World War have been popularly understood in a Euro-centric manner. But descendants of Indian soldiers and researchers have long pushed for recognition for the approximately 1.4 million men from current-day India, Pakistan and Bangladesh who helped wage the First World War for the British Empire. Yet when it comes to the war’s impact on British India, many of us still think of contributions as military and masculine. The double portrait of two Sikh risaldars, Jagat Singh and Man Singh, currently on display at the Art Gallery of Ontario is a testament to such recognition. The men hailed from Punjab, the hub of military recruitment known as the “sword arm” of the Raj. The piece was painted in London by Phillip de László two months before the Battle of the Somme in 1916, when many Indian soldiers were wounded or lost their lives. But remembrance is gendered. Historian Radhika Singha has revealed the overlooked role of non-combatants such as labourers, cooks, sweepers and many other essential “follower” roles in the war. Male and militarized remembrance also takes for granted the impact of the war on those women and families the men left behind. As my preliminary research into First World War archives of letters, songs and reports indicate, women bore the consequences of the total war thousands of miles away from the Western Front. Early on, women recognized the gendered cost of the war, and were critical of the reliance on their husbands, sons and fathers to wage it. A recruiting meeting held at one of the hill fairs in India in October 1917. (Press Agency Photographer/India during the First World War, 1914-1918/Imperial War Museums) Compounding gendered hierarchies The impact of the First World War compounded the gendered hierarchies already existing in Punjab. The state of Punjab in northern India was annexed by the East India Company in 1849. Colonial officials were keen to secure political and economic control by joining hands with existing patriarchs and landowners in this agricultural economy. First World War Hindi-language recruitment poster with slogan statement that beings: ‘This soldier defends India. He protects his home and family.’ (Imperial War Museum) But such developments were especially harmful for women. As feminist historian Veena Oldenburg has shown, measures such as the codification of customary law based on consultations with male household heads formalized the dominance of the male landowner. This contributed to making women dependent on the men around them. Colonial officials were also fascinated by the Punjabi peasant because they believed that he embodied war-like qualities. The Darwinian “martial race theory” claimed that only certain men in India could be soldiers. Colonial authorities came to view the Punjabi peasant, who worked the land and had a history of a military tradition, as fighting material. By the turn of the 20th century, these ideas culminated in what researchers termed the “Punjabization of the Indian Army.” On the eve of the First World War, about 60 per cent of the Indian army was made up of Punjabi men. When war broke out, colonial authorities promoted recruitment of local men through further promises of land grants, cash rewards and secure pay, and linked it to the ideas of izzat or honour. How did women respond to the war? While middle class and elite Indian women led campaigns to encourage wives and mothers to send their husbands and sons to war, this response wasn’t universal. Many women in the villages of Punjab tried to prevent their husbands and sons from enlisting. News and letters from the war front revealed the brutal conditions of trench warfare. According to colonial reports of the time, mothers and wives believed that men were not being adequately trained before they were sent off. The colonial government denounced such beliefs as wild rumours. Yet historical evidence shows that women in Punjab tried to hinder recruitment efforts to such an extent that, by December 1914, colonial officials complained that the “tears of womenfolk” had become the biggest hurdle to recruitment. In Amritsar, Punjab, in 1915, an official noted in his diary that women “would trail recruiting parties for several miles, patiently awaiting opportunities to lure away acquired recruits.” Colonial intelligence reports show women would sing songs blaming King George for taking away their husbands and brothers. In these, women offered trenchant critiques of the colonial government, claiming that their men had been used as fodder by the firangi (colonizer). In 2016, Berlin based Pakistani artist Bani Abidi displayed contemporary renditions of folk songs at the Edinburgh Art Festival. Entitled, “Memorial to Lost Words,” this exhibition moves beyond “stone engravings or statues” as sites of memory but combines translated letters and folk songs. Phrases from a translated folk song sing: “Don’t go, don’t go, stay here my friend, the ignorant are packing up and leaving, flowers are withering, friendships are breaking.” Bani Abidi’s Memorial to Lost Words is a sound installation bearing poignant testament to the tragedy of the First World War. Scrambling for survival Women whose husbands enlisted scrambled for money to survive. Delays in the receipt of remittances and pay added to their economic struggles. A collection of letters shows that one wife wrote to her husband in France that she had only received two months’ worth of allowances in six months and had to resort to pawning her jewellery to “keep myself alive.” Conditions had worsened because the entire economy was geared toward the war effort. Famine, plague and influenza added to the troubles. Urdu-language First World War propaganda poster reads: ‘Look at that man. He is doing his duty to his King. He is demonstrating his bravery and making his family proud as well as earning more money than before.’ (Imperial War Museums) But women did not suffer passively. They held their husbands accountable for going to the war. One woman complained to her husband: “I go round begging the neighbours for water and wood, yet you never think of all this.” Some women even used the war to run away with their lovers while their husbands were away, which troubled the men and the colonial government alike. Women’s efforts to hinder recruitment in Punjab, their critique of the colonial government and their letters reveal the complexities of women’s responses to the war. Beyond remembering the male soldier who arrived in Europe, we should also remember those he left behind. Umaima Miraj received funding from the Social Science and Humanities Research Council for this research.
