6ea945f382f18776: From Ibrahim M Ahmad
The dispute over former prime minister Najib Razak’s proposed transfer from Kajang Prison to house arrest is no longer simply about whether he should go home.

At its core, the controversy raises a broader question: what happens when a royal pardon, a court order and a separate criminal sentence intersect in ways that existing laws do not clearly anticipate?

The latest developments have placed the Attorney-General’s Chambers (AGC), the prisons department, Najib’s lawyers and even Istana Negara on seemingly different sides of a debate over implementation rather than principle. All parties say they are attempting to uphold the law. The disagreement is over what the law, and the Yang di-Pertuan Agong's decree, require in practice.
That distinction is important.

Public discussion has largely centred on whether Najib should be released from prison immediately. Yet the more significant issue may be whether Malaysia’s legal framework adequately addresses a situation in which a prisoner is granted a conditional royal pardon while also facing another custodial sentence.

The King’s position appears straightforward. Najib was granted a conditional pardon allowing him to serve the remainder of his SRC International sentence under house arrest, provided he paid the RM50 million fine imposed by the court. That condition has now been met.
Ordinarily, that would appear to settle the matter.

However, the High Court document issued following payment of the fine has introduced uncertainty over the legal effect of Najib’s "discharge" and whether the SRC sentence continues to run until 2028 or is regarded as completed.

The document, called an “Order of Discharge on Payment of Fine”, directs that Najib be discharged immediately. But it also states that the remainder of his sentence is to be served under house arrest until Aug 23, 2028.

The question is what “discharged” means in this context. Does it mean he should leave Kajang Prison and continue serving his SRC sentence at home? Or could it mean that the SRC sentence is legally complete? The AGC says clarification is needed on the effect of the order.
The distinction is far from academic.

Najib’s separate 15-year prison sentence in the 1MDB case was ordered to begin only after the SRC sentence ends. If the SRC sentence continues under house arrest, the chronology is uncomplicated. If it is deemed complete upon payment of the fine, questions arise about whether the 1MDB sentence should begin immediately.
Faced with that uncertainty, the AGC argues that clarification is needed before any transfer takes place.

Critics may see this as an unnecessary delay, particularly after Istana Negara stated that all conditions of the pardon had been fulfilled. Supporters of the AGC’s position, however, contend that resolving ambiguity now is preferable to triggering fresh legal challenges later.
Neither argument is entirely without merit.

What the episode has exposed is a potential gap in Malaysia’s legal architecture. While imprisonment, parole and remission are governed by established laws and procedures, house arrest remains relatively unfamiliar territory. There is no comprehensive statutory framework setting out how such arrangements should operate, how compliance should be monitored or how they interact with other criminal sentences.
That absence has created room for competing interpretations.

The issue also extends beyond Najib himself. Any legal principles established in his case could influence how future pardons are implemented and how exceptional forms of custody are administered. For that reason, the courts’ eventual interpretation may carry implications beyond one high-profile prisoner.
At the same time, there is a public confidence dimension that cannot be ignored.

Najib’s status as a former prime minister means every development is scrutinised through the lens of equality before the law. Many Malaysians will want assurance that whatever outcome emerges is grounded in clear legal principles rather than political considerations or institutional pressure.
That makes transparency critical.
The public deserves a clear explanation of how the pardon is meant to operate, how the prison and court orders interact, and how the separate 1MDB sentence fits into the equation.

Ultimately, the dispute should not become a contest between institutions. The King’s decree, the courts and the executive branch each have defined constitutional roles. The challenge lies in ensuring those roles operate coherently when they overlap.

The immediate question is whether Najib leaves prison or remains there for the time being. The more enduring question is whether Malaysia’s legal system can provide a clear and consistent answer when faced with circumstances that its laws did not expressly anticipate.
That is an issue that extends well beyond Najib Razak.
Ibrahim M Ahmad is an FMT reader.

51322d004c17054c: Dalam dunia politik moden yang penuh dengan kebanjiran maklumat, propaganda tidak lagi beroperasi dengan cara lama yang kasar, memaksa dan terang-terangan. Propaganda hari ini bergerak melalui bahasa, khususnya bahasa yang samar, berlapik, dan mengelirukan.

Menurut Jason Stanley, Profesor Falsafah di Yale University dan penulis buku How Propaganda Works (2015), propaganda moden berjaya bukan kerana ia mengelirukan, tetapi kerana ia menggunakan kebenaran yang difahamkan secara keliru. Bahasa propaganda menjadi alat untuk mengawal fikiran rakyat dengan cara yang lembut, hampir tidak dapat dikesan, namun sangat efektif dalam membentuk apa yang rakyat fikir benar.

Stanley menjelaskan propaganda moden berfungsi dengan cara menghalang wacana kritikal. Ia bukan sekadar menutup akses kepada maklumat, tetapi memanipulasi makna maklumat tersebut sehingga rakyat tidak dapat membuat penilaian rasional.

Bahasa yang digunakan kelihatan profesional, teknikal dan dilihat rasional namun sebenarnya ia menyembunyikan tindakan sebenar atau menutup kegagalan. Contoh mudah: apabila subsidi ditarik balik, ia akan disebut sebagai ‘penstrukturan semula mekanisme bantuan’ atau ‘rasionalisasi subsidi’. Apabila berlaku masalah dalam pentadbiran, kita mendengar frasa ‘isu dalam perhatian’, ‘penilaian sedang dibuat’, atau ‘perkara ini sedang dikaji secara menyeluruh’. Semua ayat ini nampak sopan dan meyakinkan, tetapi jika diteliti secara mendalam, ia tidak menjelaskan apa-apa pun.

Seni propaganda melalui bahasa samar ini berfungsi kerana ia memenuhi dua keperluan politik: pertama, menjaga imej pemerintah; kedua, menenangkan rakyat supaya tidak panik. Stanley membahagikan propaganda kepada dua kategori.
Supporting propaganda menggunakan bahasa yang kelihatan menyokong nilai demokrasi seperti ketelusan, profesionalisme dan kestabilan, tetapi tujuan sebenarnya ialah mengekalkan kuasa pemerintah.

Undermining propaganda pula ialah bahasa yang kelihatan rasional tetapi digunakan untuk menutup ketidakjujuran atau tindakan yang bertentangan dengan kepentingan awam. Kedua-duanya menggunakan bahasa yang sama iaitu kabur, berlapik, dan sabar berfungsi dalam konteks yang berbeza.

Dalam masyarakat moden, bahasa berlapik digunakan untuk mengurus persepsi dan emosi rakyat. Apabila isu sensitif timbul seperti kenaikan harga barang, kegagalan projek mega, kelemahan institusi, atau ketegangan kaum, pemerintah cenderung memilih frasa-frasa yang menenangkan. ‘Mengawal tekanan ekonomi global’, ‘menyelaraskan semula struktur fiskal’, ‘memperkukuh ekosistem pentadbiran’, atau ‘melakukan penambahbaikan proses’. Semuanya adalah contoh bagaimana bahasa digunakan untuk melunakkan realiti. Rakyat mendengar perkataan yang sedap, tetapi tidak memahami apakah tindakan sebenar yang sedang dilakukan.

Stanley menegaskan propaganda moden juga bekerja melalui kebanjiran maklumat. Dalam sistem di mana media dikawal secara langsung atau tidak langsung, maklumat satu sisi menjadi norma. Rakyat bergantung kepada ‘kebenaran rasmi’, dan bahasa pemerintah menjadi bahasa media.

Maka. gaya bahasa berlapik yang sama diulang melalui berita, kenyataan akhbar, laporan ekonomi dan ucapan pemimpin. Ulangan ini akhirnya menjadikan bahasa propaganda sebagai bahasa biasa. Rakyat tidak menyedari mereka sedang dipengaruhi, kerana bahasa yang digunakan bukan bahasa kasar atau menipu, tetapi bahasa yang nampak profesional.

Bahasa samar juga digunakan untuk mencipta musuh yang tidak bernama. Teknik ini sangat berkesan kerana ia menanam emosi tanpa perlu membuktikan apa-apa. Ungkapan seperti ‘pihak tertentu sedang cuba menggugat kestabilan negara’, ‘agenda asing sedang menyusup’, atau ‘unsur ekstrem tidak boleh dipandang ringan’ sering digunakan tanpa identiti jelas.

Rakyat mendengar ancaman, merasai kebimbangan, tetapi tidak mengetahui siapa musuh sebenar. Inilah teknik propaganda yang menanam rasa takut secara terkawal dan sekali gus memberikan justifikasi kepada tindakan pemerintah untuk bertindak keras, menggubal undang-undang tambahan atau mengawal ruang awam.

Dalam konteks Malaysia, budaya bahasa berlapik sudah lama berakar. Ketika isu perkauman timbul, istilah ‘sensitiviti masyarakat’ digunakan untuk mengelakkan perbincangan terus tentang diskriminasi atau ketidaksamarataan.

Ketika berlaku skandal, istilah ‘ketirisan kecil’ digunakan. Ketika ekonomi merosot, istilah ‘penyesuaian struktur ekonomi’ menjadi pilihan. Apabila kerajaan gagal mengurus bencana, ungkapan ‘cabaran penyelarasan’ digunakan bagi mengalihkan perhatian daripada kelemahan pengurusan. Bahasa ini tidak salah, tetapi ia menjarakkan rakyat daripada memahami realiti sebenar.

Propaganda melalui bahasa samar bekerja bukan dengan cara memaksa rakyat percaya sesuatu, tetapi dengan cara mengisi ruang antara penjelasan dan kekeliruan. Rakyat yang tidak mendapat maklumat sebenar akhirnya membina naratif sendiri berdasarkan andaian dan perasaan.

Inilah yang dimaksudkan Stanley apabila beliau mengatakan propaganda moden adakalanya memanipulasi rasional manusia. Ia mengehadkan rakyat untuk berfikir, tetapi mendidik mereka menerima kabus sebagai kebenaran.

Dalam era digital, bahasa samar menjadi lebih penting kerana maklumat tersebar dengan pantas. Propagandis perlu mengurus persepsi dengan cepat, dan bahasa berlapik memberikan mereka masa. Satu kenyataan kabur sudah cukup untuk menghentikan kritikan selama 24 jam, sementara strategi komunikasi seterusnya disusun. Contohnya, ketika berlaku masalah dalam sesuatu operasi kenyataan seperti ‘sistem sedang dipertingkatkan’ atau ‘masalah teknikal sedang diselesaikan’ membantu menutup tekanan awam sementara ruang masa dicari boleh menyelesaikan masalah.

Kesannya, rakyat berdepan dunia yang penuh dengan ayat tetapi kosong makna. Mereka mendengar banyak perkataan, tetapi sedikit fakta. Mereka rasa diberi maklumat, tetapi sebenarnya menerima secara samar. Propaganda paling berjaya ialah propaganda yang menjadikan rakyat percaya mereka memahami sesuatu isu padahal mereka tidak diberi maklumat sebenar.

Jason Stanley merumuskan hal ini dengan tepat iaitu: ‘Propaganda ialah manipulasi kehendak rasional manusia sehingga perbincangan terhenti’. Inilah kekuatan gaya bahasa samar dan berlapik. Ia bukan hanya menutup kebenaran, tetapi menutup pintu untuk bertanya.
Dan selama pintu itu tertutup, propaganda menguasai seluruh ruang pemikiran masyarakat.

c6e7cabff185da96: An extract from Plato's "Republic" reads: "Said the old Cephalus to the younger Socrates, 'Older men of my age flock together and in our meeting my common tale is – I cannot eat, I cannot drink, the pleasure of youth and love have fled away, there was a good time once, but now gone, and life is no longer ours.'"
Such is the reality of ageing, and perhaps there is a lesson here for politicians who have overstayed their welcome in the political arena.
I hope that the impending Melaka state election will be an eye-opener for Malaysians, particularly our political leaders who seem to have difficulty recognising when it is time to call it a day.
PAS president Abdul Hadi Awang and many politicians of his generation should seriously consider retiring from politics.
Judging from their regular outbursts and political pronouncements, some appear increasingly disconnected from the realities, aspirations and concerns of ordinary Malaysians.
Their political vocabulary, arguments and preoccupations seem to belong to another era.
Hadi's latest outburst is a case in point.
In his reaction to the confidence and supply agreement (CSA) between opposition MPs and the government, he likened the arrangement to the deception of the Dajjal.

Whatever one's views about the CSA, surely there are more constructive ways to debate a parliamentary arrangement. It is one thing to disagree with a political agreement; it is quite another to invoke apocalyptic religious imagery to discredit it.
Such rhetoric does little to advance public understanding or the quality of our political discourse.
Malaysia is rapidly changing
This is precisely the problem with some of our ageing political leaders. They seem more interested in fighting yesterday's political battles than addressing tomorrow's challenges.
Our younger population is concerned about employment, housing affordability, wages, education, technology, artificial intelligence, green agenda and the rising cost of living.
They want practical solutions, economic opportunities and a government that understands the world they are growing up in.
Yet much of our political conversation remains trapped in old rivalries, identity politics, religious arguments and endless disputes over who should be in power and who should become prime minister.
How much longer must Malaysians listen to identity and religious politics from the same personalities with the same political arguments?

Hadi is not alone. Former prime minister Muhyiddin Yassin, deputy prime minister Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, former federal minister Rais Yatim and several other long-serving political figures should seriously consider leaving the political arena as well.

They have had their opportunities, occupied important positions and exercised considerable influence over the country's political upheavals. They should recognise that political leadership is not a lifetime entitlement.

There is a difference between serving the country and holding on to political power. After decades in politics, surely there comes a time when personal ambition must give way to institutional renewal.

Our political parties should not be personal properties, nor should their leadership positions become permanent appointments. No individual should be indispensable to a political party, let alone to an entire nation.
Malaysia's political weakness

One of Malaysia's biggest political weaknesses is the reluctance of senior politicians to groom and give way to younger leaders. They continue to dominate party structures, determine candidate selections and control political narratives.
Young politicians are often expected to wait patiently for their turn, while the same senior personalities continue to occupy the top positions election after election.
This is unhealthy.
A political party cannot produce new leaders or renew its leadership in a hierarchy that is dominated by ageing politicians. PAS, Bersatu and Umno are clear examples.
Do they genuinely believe in the future of their parties or are they simply protecting their own positions?
I fully agree with the argument about giving younger politicians greater opportunities.

The emergence of younger leaders should not merely be an electoral gimmick to attract younger voters. They must be given real responsibilities, decision-making authority and opportunities to shape national policies.
Of course, being young does not automatically make someone a capable leader. Experience, integrity, competence and sound judgment matter.

But these qualities cannot be the exclusive possessions of older politicians, either. Young leaders need opportunities to acquire experience, and they cannot do so if the older generation refuses to release its grip.

Let the younger generation make mistakes, learn from them and develop their own leadership capabilities. That is how political maturity is built. We cannot keep telling young people that they lack experience while denying them the opportunity to gain it.

There is also a larger democratic question. How can we expect a country to embrace new ideas, modernise its institutions and prepare for the future when much of its political leadership remains occupied by personalities whose political careers began several decades ago?
The world is moving on
Technology, economic structures, international competition and the expectations of younger citizens are changing. Political leadership must change with them.
For Hadi, Muhyiddin, Zahid and scores of others who have spent much of their lives in politics, perhaps the greatest contribution they can now make is to step aside gracefully.

They can offer advice, share their experience and allow the next generation to take responsibility. They do not need to remain party presidents, political kingmakers or permanent fixtures in our national politics.

The Melaka election should be more than another contest between political coalitions. It should also be an opportunity for voters to consider the kind of leadership they want for the next decade and beyond.

Malaysia needs a political generation that looks forward, not backwards; one that debates policies rather than personalities, solves problems rather than manufactures controversies, and builds institutions rather than protects individual political careers.
Enough is enough. You have had your time. You have had your opportunities. It is time to let go.

3b237e183dd5187e: Malaysians have come to take our festivals for granted, gliding through Deepavali as if it were just another ordinary day on the calendar—a polite pause amid the roar of traffic and the clatter of daily life.

Yet, if we close our eyes for a moment and picture it—houses alive with oil lamps glowing in every direction, the air fragrant with sesame-scented murukku, and the laughter of children in new clothes spilling onto the streets—we are reminded of the festival's vibrant soul.
What few of us realise, however, is that this radiant celebration once rose in daring rebellion.
Today, Deepavali burns brightly as a public holiday across Peninsular Malaysia, with Sabah having quietly folded it into its own calendar of observances.

But few know the breathless, dramatic saga of how this festival was once locked in a fierce, cinematic battle for supremacy—not merely over lamps and sweets, but for the very right to be recognised as a national holiday.
That epic contest was fought not against external forces, but between two towering pillars of the Hindu community itself: Deepavali and Thaipusam.

Both claimed the same prize: a full public holiday so their celebrations could soar to their unbridled heights. One side believed Deepavali, with its blaze of lights that welcomed every soul under the sun, was the broader, more inclusive flame that would carry Indian identity into the future. The other saw in Thaipusam—with its profound message of inner victory through devotion and discipline—the sacred, undying fire that needed to be nurtured.
The battle was real, heated, and decided in colonial Singapore in 1914—a moment that still echoes today, though almost all of us remain blissfully unaware of it.
I wonder how many Malaysians—Indians among them—know that the first Indian-related public holiday in British Malaya was actually for Thaipusam?

Then spelled Tai-pusum, it first flickered into existence in the 1879 Holidays Ordinance IX as a bank holiday in Penang. In British Malaya, bank holidays existed primarily to ensure the colony's commercial engine paused simultaneously.

Thaipusam secured its spot because of a dynamic Indian merchant class in Penang and because government departments, most notably the Public Works Department and the municipal council, were overwhelmingly staffed by Indians.

Then came 1914. The colonial administration decided that one set of uniform public holidays should cover the entire Straits Settlements. Operating under the rule of "one major festival of each of the main races," a Bill was drafted nominating Thaipusam for the Indian community as it was already a holiday in Penang.

Here the story takes a twist. The English-speaking elites and merchants of Singapore preferred Deepavali. Their community was a diverse tapestry woven from Telugus, Gujaratis, Sindhis, Malayalees, and Punjabis—not just Tamils. Thaipusam, they argued, was too narrow, too tied to the Chettiar community, and too purely religious for their cosmopolitan vision.
Led by the formidable Dr N Veerasamy Naidu—one of Singapore’s first Indian doctors and a municipal commissioner—the merchant group petitioned Governor Sir Arthur Henderson Young.

Their letter glowed with eloquence and loyalty, speaking of making Deepavali “an act of grace which will be greatly appreciated not only by the 60 or 70,000 most loyal and submissive subjects of His most gracious Majesty the Emperor of India but by the future generations of the permanent residents of the colony”.
They reminded the governor that Deepavali was already observed as a public holiday in India and that it was a public holiday in Singapore in the year 1912.

The movement quickly gained momentum. In February 1914, roughly a thousand prominent Hindus packed the Hindu Association on Belilios Road. Veerasamy, who chaired the meeting, reminded those present that Deepavali had been declared a holiday in Singapore in 1912, thanks to an earlier petition through the Hindu and Muhammadan Endowments Board. Yet a similar application in 1913 had not succeeded.
Now the stakes were higher — the holiday would cover the whole colony. And it would not require annual petitions.

Among those present were influential merchants and elites such as MV Pillay, SMR Naidu, KN Kothary, Nagar Das, Chotiirmal, M Soomapah, Mungul Singh, Dr Bardhan, Veer Singh, Thambyrajah, Veeraragava Aiyar, Singaram Pillai and Sivakadacha Padayachi.

Leaders like MV Pillay argued passionately that Deepavali suited Singapore’s multi-racial fabric better, allowing other races to share in its social joy, whereas Thaipusam remained a strictly intense, specialised Hindu observance.

Noting that Deepavali was a public holiday in India, Pillay insisted the same should apply in the Straits Settlements of Singapore, Penang and Malacca (now Melaka). He added that Indian workers in the PWD and municipal council in Singapore were usually given a holiday on Deepavali day and not Thaipusam day.

The meeting adopted a proposal to send a delegation to convince Governor Young to make Deepavali the public holiday for Hindus in the colony. MV Pillay, who moved the motion, claimed that it was the Chettiar community that was pushing for Thaipusam, and that in doing so it had disregarded the wishes of other communities.

Not everyone agreed with this resolution. Some Singapore Hindus, including those not from the Chettiar community, wrote directly to the governor insisting the original Bill remain unchanged. They claimed that Veerasamy’s group did not speak for everyone and that the government would earn the deep gratitude of the community by following Penang's example.

A fierce but polite battle ensued between supporters of both festivals. Ultimately, the British authorities chose to listen to the Singapore merchant class and the more influential English-speaking elites.
They dropped Thaipusam from the Bill and substituted it with Deepavali, passing the Holidays (Amendment) Ordinance 1914 for the entire colony of Singapore, Penang, and Malacca.

I was unable to find any record that showed strong protests from Penang and Malacca Hindus. I suspect the Chettiars - a small, self-reliant and self-effacing mercantile community that prefers to conduct its business in quiet dignity - decided that Thaipusam would still be observed with due respect even if it was no longer an official holiday.

But the ripple effect soon reached the Federated Malay States (FMS). By April 1915, KT Parmanan Pillay, president of the Sri Mahamariamman Temple on High Street (Jalan Tun HS Lee), wrote to Selangor Resident Edward George Broadrick, telling him that the local Hindu community had passed a resolution asking for both Thaipusam and Deepavali to be declared public holidays.

In Taiping, then the capital of Perak, a public meeting was held in the town hall on Feb 21, 1926 under the chairmanship of H Rethinasamy Pillai, reportedly attended by Indians from several parts of the FMS. The meeting resolved to urge the British authorities to also make Deepavali a public holiday in the FMS, as there was then none for the community.

One of the leaders, V Murugasu Pillai, in a letter to the chief secretary to the FMS government Sir William George Maxwell, noted that Deepavali was already a holiday in the neighbouring Straits Settlements. He claimed that the views of the “Indian and Ceylonese communities” in Selangor, Negri Sembilan and Pahang had also been obtained and that all of them were unanimous in voicing the request for a holiday for Deepavali.

Whether the colonial authorities fully capitulated back then remains slightly murky in the archives, but the framework of history eventually birthed the national holiday we enjoy today under the 1951 Holidays Act.
Today, Deepavali’s lights burn brightly across Malaysia, while in several states, Thaipusam remains a powerful public holiday observed with equal vitality.

Ultimately, the story of Deepavali’s rise is one of quiet endurance rather than conquest. Two great flames once stood at opposite ends of the Hindu night sky—one broad and welcoming, the other focused and sacred. Colonial hands chose one over the other a century ago, but time has proven that neither had to be extinguished.

Today, both Deepavali and Thaipusam light up the Malaysian landscape side by side, proving that traditions fought for with such passion never truly fade. They simply learn to glow together, year after year, across the same land.
Happy Deepavali.

<!--kg-card-end: html--> Welcome back to the Abstract! Here are the studies this week that drew a blank, felt the squeeze, played the queen, and made donkey-bull love.

First, scientists shed new light on how Earth ended up losing more than a billion years of its geological record, a puzzle that has resisted explanation for decades. Then: octopuses in tight spots, a topless spear-brandishing Celt, and a tale of unlikely tail.
As always, for more of my work, check out my book First Contact: The Story of Our Obsession with Aliens, or subscribe to my personal newsletter The BeX Files.
“Blank Space” (Earth’s Version)
Dhungana, Santosh and Flament, Nicolas. “The deep Earth origin of the Great Unconformity. Nature.

Earth doesn’t trouble itself too much with keeping intact archives. With its tectonic activity and erosive forces, our planet is constantly wiping out huge chunks of its own memory, creating gaps in the geological record called unconformities.

The Great Unconformity, the largest gap of this kind, reveals that Earth straight-up deleted more than a billion years of strata, for reasons that remain hotly debated and mysterious. Sandstone that dates back to the Cambrian period some 538 million years is often found directly on top of ancient “basement” rocks that date back anywhere from 1.2 billion to 1.8 billion years ago. This missing layer shows up around the world, hinting that it was erased by a global event.
Now, scientists have placed the origins of the Great Unconformity deep inside Earth’s mantle, during the tectonic tumult of supercontinent breakup.

“The cause or causes of the Great Unconformity are unknown,” said authors Santosh Dhungana and Nicolas Flament of the University of Wollongong. “The proposed mechanisms include extensive glacial erosion during Snowball Earth (about 720–635 million years ago), rifting and plume activity, sea-level fall and mantle-driven dynamic topography.”
“These processes have not been dynamically tested, with limited comparison between global models and global datasets to explain the spatial distribution of the Great Unconformity,” the team added.

To fill the knowledge gap about the geological gap, the researchers ran models of the formation and breakup of ancient supercontinents during the eons preceding the Cambrian period, when complex life rapidly proliferated in Earth’s seas. Massive landmasses were pushed upward by motions in Earth’s mantle during this time. Exposed to erosive forces such as weather, glaciers, and eventually oceans, they became sanded down over time, creating the vast void.

“Our models explain why the Great Unconformity is best preserved in North America and show that it is a first-order surface expression of deep geodynamic processes that transformed global landscapes and sediment fluxes,” the team concluded.

Scientists will no doubt continue to debate the cause of this planet-wide memory lapse, but there is consensus that the same mechanisms also set the stage for the emergence of complex life during the Cambrian. No matter what caused the Great Unconformity, we partly owe our existence to it today.
In other news…
Putting the squeeze on octopuses
Xin, Wenci et al. “Overcoming environmental constraints: octopus uses 3-step or 4-step strategies to squeeze through small holes.” Journal of Experimental Biology.

We’ll move now from massive gaps in Earth’s memory to tiny gaps that octopuses can somehow squeeze through. These tentacled escape artists can famously maneuver their way through passages that seem impossibly small relative to their bodies, an ability that has spawned a subgenre of viral videos.

Now, scientists have discovered the secrets of “octopus-squeezing behavior” by observing two species—the common octopus (Octopus vulgaris) and the Mayan octopus (Octopus maya)—navigating small holes in laboratory containers.

“Our study demonstrates that octopuses employ two primary strategies, 3-step and 4-step, for squeezing through narrow spaces,” said researchers led by Wenci Xin of the National University of Singapore. “The key distinction between these strategies lies in whether the body is squeezed separately from the arms.”

The first two steps were probing the aperture and then shifting a few arms through it. Navigating the tightest spaces required breaking up the final passage into two parts: Pulling the remaining arms to the other side, and then compressing the mantle behind the head so they could fit through last.
In addition to documenting these amazing feats of flexibility in nature, the study is the perfect excuse to revisit the classic X-Files episode “Squeeze.”
A queen hidden in plain sight?
Russell, Miles. “Verica Rex: Searching for a ‘lost’ queen of the British Iron Age.” Current Archaeology.

When Rome invaded Britain 2,000 years ago, they had the help of an inside man—or was it an inside woman? In a new article, an archaeologist makes the case that the British king Verica, who aided the Roman invasion of their own homeland, was actually a queen that has been misgendered lo these many centuries.

Miles Russell of Bournemouth University argues that Verica was a woman based in part on the leader’s Latin name, which ends in the suffix “a” which is common for women, as opposed to names ending in “-us” for men.

Coins also depict Verica using “slender, bare-breasted equestrian figures that appear irrefutably female in contrast to the overtly masculine warriors on the issues of Iron Age rulers like Tasciovanus and Caratacus,” according to Russell.

Many experts are not convinced that the evidence points to a secret ancient queen, and Verica’s gender is likely to inspire much more debate. Wikipedia, our great public arbiter, has not changed Verica’s male pronouns.

Women leaders weren’t unheard of in Celtic Britain, as evidenced by the queens Cartimandua and Boudica, who lived in the same century as Verica. Regardless of whether Verica was among their ranks, this leader was a consequential figure in the Roman takeover of Britain.
Achille and Patroclo: More than friends
Da Cruz, André B et al. “A socio-sexual bond between a bull and a male donkey.” Current Biology.
Scientists who were conducting fieldwork on monkeys in Ethiopia serendipitously stumbled upon a very different discovery—a tender same-sex relationship between a bull and a donkey.

Achille, a bull, and Patroclo, a donkey, belong to different owners, but they graze together by day. Despite the availability of other males and females in their pasture, this pair has developed a strong socio-sexual bond that includes nuzzling, licking, and Achille sexually mounting Patroclo.

“Patroclo frequently presented his hindquarters toward Achille and nipped him,” said researchers led by André Beirão da Cruz of the University of Pisa. “In the only two instances in which Achille approached and mounted another male donkey, this individual showed clear avoidance behaviours and displayed threatening facial expressions (e.g. ear flattening), which were never observed in Patroclo during the 51 mountings (34 with intromission) with Achille.”

Same-sex sexual behavior is extremely common in nature and has a wide variety of possible explanations, including social cohesion, mistaken identity, or lack of access to opposite-sex mates. But what Achille and Patroclo have is special. Despite being different species and having alternate mating options, the pair share a highly selective and reciprocal social and sexual bond.

“Although interpreting this behaviour is challenging, the mounting attempts, taken together with the repeated and mutual affiliative interactions between the two animals, may signal the quality of their relationship” and “the strength of the animals’ social bond,” the team concluded.

In addition to this heartwarming tale, the study goes to show that you never know what you might find when you chase your goals. The researchers were there to watch geladas, but it turned out those primates weren’t the only animals monkeying around.
Thanks for reading! See you next week.
